A distinctive, painful, benign osteoblastic bone tumor
Epidemiology
Demographics
The male-to-female ratio is 3:1.
Most patients are aged 5 to 25 years.

Epidemiology
Osteoid osteoma is the most common benign bone-forming tumor. It accounts for 3% of
all primary bone tumors, and 10% to 12% of all benign bone tumors analyzed via biopsy.
In more than 50% of patients, the lesion is localized to the metaphysis and diaphysis of
long bones (especially the femur and tibia). Other less common sites of involvement
include the posterior elements of the spine and the upper extremity. Lesions can be
entirely intracortical or may involve the endosteal or periosteal surfaces of bone
(Resource 1). Peak incidence is in individuals in their teenage years, with 80% of tumors
occurring in patients aged 5 to 25 years . Males are more commonly affected than
females.1
Etiology
Genetics/etiology
Thought to be related to rearrangements in FOS or FOSB

Etiology
With whole-genome DNA and RNA sequencing of bone tumors, recurrent
rearrangements of FOS (chromosome 14) or FOSB (chromosome 19) have been shown in
osteoid osteoma and osteoblastoma. This has been further supported via fluorescence
in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry in histology specimens.1

Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History
Clinical presentation
Classic symptom is night pain relieved by aspirin or NSAIDs.
The pain is progressive in its severity, can be referred to an adjacent joint, and may be
present for months to years before diagnosis.
Most common locations include the femur, tibia, vertebral arch, humerus, and fingers. The
proximal femur is the most common site; the hip is the most common intra-articular
location.
Osteoid osteomas usually occur in the diaphyseal or metaphyseal regions of long bones.
If an osteoid osteoma is the cause of a painful scoliosis, the lesion usually is at the center of
the concavity of the curve.
Osteoid osteomas can cause extensive inflammatory symptoms in the adjacent tissues (joint
effusions, contractures, limp, muscle atrophy).
High levels of prostaglandins and cyclooxygenase are produced by the tumor.

Patient History
Patients with osteoid osteoma present with a common/classic pain pattern that is
quickly yet temporarily alleviated via the administration of NSAIDs and/or aspirin.
Patients often will present with months of pain that may be present at rest or at night,
which helps distinguish this entity from mechanical symptoms. The mechanism via which
aspirin and NSAIDs alleviate pain from osteoid osteomas is explained by the production
of prostaglandin E2 and prostacyclin by the tumor. Through the inhibition of
cyclooxygenase enzymes (COX-1 and COX-2), these medications block the production of
prostaglandins. The clinician should question the diagnosis of osteoid osteoma in the
absence of night pain and/or response to NSAIDs. An osteoid osteoma that presents
adjacent to or within a joint may mimic monoarticular inflammatory arthritis because the
patient may present with a joint effusion and stiffness. Reactive scoliosis may result from
an axial lesion, which is commonly observed in the posterior elements of the spine.
During history acquisition, patients often are able to precisely localize the lesion based
on the location of their pain; however, a lesion located adjacent to a major nerve may

osteoid osteoma located in the pelvis).1
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Round, well-circumscribed intracortical lesion with radiolucent nidus
Lesions usually less than 1 cm in diameter
Extensive, benign periosteal reaction that may obscure the nidus
Occasionally, lesions are subchondral, subperiosteal, or medullary; these cause less
surrounding periosteal reaction.
Radiographic differential diagnosis includes osteomyelitis, Ewing sarcoma, Brodie abscess,
osteoblastoma, and stress fracture.1
CT
Thin-cut CT scans often are the key to diagnosis because they frequently identify the small
radiolucent nidus.
Often demonstrates abundant reactive bone formation
MRI
MRI often shows extensive surrounding edema but may not show a discrete nidus because
of the thickness of cuts.
Bone scintigraphy
Intense and focal increased tracer uptake in the surrounding bone on Tc-99m bone scan

Imaging Studies
On plain radiographs, osteoid osteoma is characterized by a small lucent central region
(typically <1 cm) of fibroosseous tumor surrounded by a zone of reactive bone sclerosis.
This results in the characteristic radiographic lesion referred to as a nidus (Figure 1).
Thin-cut CT scans often are necessary to visualize the nidus and its relationship to
surrounding bone because lesions often are very small. A substantial amount of cortical
reaction often is observed around the nidus (Figures 2 through 4). MRI often is less
helpful than CT because the osteoid osteoma can mimic a malignant or infectious

because of the inflammatory action of robust prostaglandin production (Figure 5).
Localization of a nidus can be aided by nuclear imaging studies, such as a technetium Tc-
99m bone scan (Figure 6). This imaging modality is helpful in patients with referred pain
that obscures the anatomic location of the lesion; however, bone scans often are not
necessary in the work up of an osteoid osteoma given the classic presentation and
features on routine axial imaging studies.1

Trabeculae are lined with uniform, plump osteoblasts.
A 1- to 2-mm fibrovascular rim surrounds the sharply demarcated nidus.
No pleomorphic cells are present.
The lesion does not infiltrate the surrounding bone.

Pathology
The gross pathology of the radiolucent center of a nidus often appears as a red, soft,
friable tissue that can be easily separated from the surrounding sclerotic bone (Figure
7). Histologically, the nidus is characterized by an osteoid matrix with an interlacing
arrangement of osteoblast-lined trabeculae (Figure 8). Cement lines are common and
calcification of the osteoid may be prominent. Scattered multinucleated giant cells are
commonly observed. Richly vascular connective tissue devoid of hematopoietic elements
is characteristic of the intertrabecular stroma.1

Management
Nonsurgical management
Management/outcome
Long-term medical management with aspirin or NSAIDs is useful to relieve symptoms
because these lesions are self-limiting and burn out after a mean of 3 years.
Surgical management
Management/outcome
Accessible lesions typically are managed via outpatient percutaneous radiofrequency
ablation (RFA) of the lesion. A CT-guided probe is inserted into the lesion with the
temperature raised to 194°F (90°C) for 4 to 6 minutes to produce a 1-cm zone of necrosis.
Recurrence rates after RFA are less than 10%.
Contraindications
Lesions in close proximity to the neurovascular bundle or articular cartilage
Lesions localized to a superficial location (eg, tibia)
Surgical resection or burring are rarely performed if the lesion is accessible to perform RFA.
Depending on the age of the child and the duration of symptoms, removal of an osteoid
osteoma associated with a painful scoliosis will allow for resolution of the curve without
additional management.

Management
Administration of aspirin or NSAIDs is a justifiable first-line treatment option because
these drugs can effectively relieve pain, which typically is the presenting and most
bothersome patient symptom (Resource 2). Some lesions have been found to resolve
and burn out over time; however, this may be after many years.
Indications for percutaneous management of an osteoid osteoma include severe pain
that is unresponsive to medications and patients unwilling to accept long-term medical
treatment because of the potential for gastrointestinal complications associated with the
chronic use of NSAIDs. The most common percutaneous treatment options include CT-
guided percutaneous excision and CT-guided RFA (Figure 9). En bloc resection or open
curettage is infrequently performed because of the success of less invasive, image-
guided procedures.
Figure 9 Treatment algorithm for the management of osteoid osteoma and

EH, Peyser A, Mankin H: Osteoid osteoma and osteoblastoma. J Am Acad Orthop Surg

RFA is performed by using heat to destroy the nidus. This often is performed by an
interventional radiologist because of the frequent need for CT (Figure 10). This is done
by introducing the radiofrequency probe into the nidus through a cannulated needle
under CT-guided imaging. The temperature at the tip of the probe is raised to
approximately 194°F (90°C) and maintained at that level for 4 to 6 minutes.
Complications associated with RFA include incomplete ablation of the lesion, recurrence,
fracture of the managed bone (particularly around the hip joint), and damage to
overlying skin or adjacent tissues.
CT-guided percutaneous excision is performed by inserting a cannulated curet into the
lesion over a Kirschner wire under CT guidance to excise the nidus. This technique has
been reported to result in a high clinical success rate and minimal complications and
avoids complications related to the area effect of RFA.
Other less commonly used percutaneous techniques include image-guided cryotherapy,
drill trephination with or without ethanol injection, thermal destruction via laser
photocoagulation, and arthroscopic excision of juxta-articular lesions.

Osteoblastoma
Overview
A rare, aggressive, benign osteoblastic tumor
Epidemiology
Demographics
The male-to-female ratio is 2:1.
Osteoblastomas are much less common than osteoid osteomas.
Most patients are aged 10 to 30 years.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:34 AM
AAOS | Bone-Producing Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002074
16/73

Etiology
Genetics/etiology
Recurrent rearrangements of FOS and FOSB are reported.

Overview
Osteoblastoma is a lytic, fibroosseous bone tumor that produces osteoid matrix.1 It is a
benign and locally aggressive tumor and does not have malignant or metastatic
potential; however, a variant of osteosarcoma may histologically resemble
osteoblastoma (osteoblastoma-like osteosarcoma).
Osteoblastomas account for less than 1% of bone tumors analyzed via biopsy. Patients
with osteoblastoma typically are slightly older than patients with osteoid osteoma.1
Osteoblastoma is commonly observed in the axial skeleton, with more than 50% of
lesions involving the posterior elements of the spine, sacrum, and skull. Lesions found in
the appendicular skeleton have a similar distribution to that observed with osteoid
osteoma. Osteoblastomas commonly involve cancellous (medullary) bone, whereas
osteoid osteomas frequently involve the cortex.
Osteoblastomas have recurrent rearrangement of FOS (chromosome 14) or FOSB
(chromosome 19) as shown via whole-genome DNA/RNA sequencing, fluorescence in
situ hybridization, and immunohistochemistry.1 This also is observed in osteoid
osteoma.
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History
Clinical presentation
Slowly progressive, dull, aching pain of long duration; less severe than pain from an osteoid
osteoma
Night pain is not typical, and aspirin/NSAID therapy does not classically relieve symptoms.

Neurologic symptoms can occur because the spine (posterior elements) is the most common
location of osteoblastoma.
Other locations include the diaphysis or metaphysis of long bones (tibia and femur) and the
mandible.
Related swelling, muscle atrophy, and a limp may occur because the lesions are large and
present for a prolonged period.

Patient History
Osteoblastoma is clinically differentiated from osteoid osteoma via lack of the classic
night symptoms/pain relieved by NSAIDs. Other common clinical manifestations are local
tenderness and swelling, which are most notable if the tumor is near the surface. Gait
disturbance can be observed in children with involvement of the lower extremities.
Patients with osteoblastoma may present with neurologic symptoms (numbness,
tingling, radicular pain, and paresthesias) because of spinal cord or nerve root
compression.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiolucent lesion larger than 2 cm in size with occasional intralesional densities
Two-thirds of osteoblastomas are cortically based; one-third of osteoblastomas are
medullary.
Expansive with extension into the surrounding soft tissues and a rim of reactive bone around
the lesion
25% of osteoblastomas have an aggressive appearance and may be mistaken for
malignancies.
Radiographic differential diagnosis includes osteosarcoma, aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC),
osteomyelitis, and osteoid osteoma.
CT and MRI
Three-dimensional imaging studies are necessary to fully evaluate the extent of the lesion
before surgical management.

Imaging Studies
Osteoblastoma has a radiographic appearance similar to that of osteoid osteoma
(Figure 11). It has a central, well-defined lytic area surrounded by a sclerotic, reactive
border of bone. The lytic area exceeds 1.5 cm in size, which frequently is used to
distinguish it from the smaller osteoid osteoma. Another feature distinguishing an
osteoblastoma from an osteoid osteoma is less reactive bone sclerosis and more cortical
expansion.

an osteoblastoma of the medial metadiaphyseal junction characterized by a well-

formation. (Reproduced from Henshaw RM, Carmody EE: Benign bone-forming tumors,
in Biermann JS, Siegel G, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed
4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 125-140.)
Radiographic appearance usually is not diagnostic, and additional imaging studies are
required to establish a diagnosis.1 Cortical destruction and subsequent periosteal
reaction may be present in patients with relatively small lesions. This may mimic an
osteosarcoma.1 Spinal osteoblastomas predominantly arise from the posterior elements
of the spine. This may result in cortical thinning and destructive expansion of the bone
(Figure 12). A secondary ABC may occur within an osteoblastoma, which results in bone
destruction and rapid enlargement in size.1

CT is the preferred imaging modality (Figure 13). It provides the most specific
information on the location, extent, size, and nature of the lesion. CT delineates areas of
mineralization within the lesion, cortical destruction, and soft-tissue extension. The
appearance of osteoblastoma on CT scans is characterized by areas of central
mineralization, expansile bone remodeling, and signs of reactive sclerosis toward the
periphery with a thin marginal bone shell.1
Figure 13 Axial CT scan of an osteoblastoma of the distal femur shows the presence of
osteoid matrix (arrow) that could not be appreciated on plain radiographs. Note the
substantial reactive bone formation surrounding the central lesion. (Reproduced from
Henshaw RM, Carmody EE: Benign bone-forming tumors, in Biermann JS, Siegel G, eds:
Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 125-140.)
The utility of MRI in the diagnosis of osteoblastoma is questionable. MRI may
overestimate the extent of the tumor because of the increased local inflammatory

reaction and extensive marrow edema. This may mimic a more aggressive or malignant
lesion. MRI can be a valuable imaging modality in patients in whom the lesion has
extensive mass effects on the spinal canal and the spinal cord. MRI may show intra-
osseous and extraosseous reactive changes and soft-tissue infiltration. Osteoblastoma
generally appears as a low or intermediate signal intensity on T1-weighted MRIs and an
intermediate to high signal intensity on T2-weighted MRIs.1
Pathology
Histology is similar to that of an osteoid osteoma.
Irregular seams of osteoid separated by loose fibrovascular stroma are observed.
Osteoid is rimmed by prominent osteoblasts that occasionally are large and epithelioid.
Most commonly, a clear demarcation from the normal surrounding bone is observed.
10% to 40% are associated with secondary ABC formation.
Numerous mitotic figures may be present, but they are not atypical.
Differentiation of osteoblastoma from osteosarcoma, giant cell tumor, and ABC is important.
The microscopic features of osteoblastoma and osteoid osteoma are similar. Centrally, an
interlacing arrangement of bony trabeculae within a loose fibrous vascular stroma rimmed by a
single row of benign osteoblasts that are responsible for osteoid formation typically are observed
(Figure 14).

A variable number of multinucleated giant cells can be observed, which may cause some
confusion in patients with a giant cell tumor of bone. The stroma typically is characterized by a
less organized pattern of osteoid and trabecular bone distribution compared with osteoid
osteoma. Greater vascularity also may be observed. Secondary ABC degeneration may result
from the increased vascularity of the lesion. The mitotic rate may be high in focal areas, but
atypical cells should not be observed.1
Management
Nonsurgical management
Surgical management
Management/outcome
Osteoblastoma is not self-limiting and requires surgical management.
In most patients, curettage and bone grafting is adequate to achieve local control.
Nerve roots should be maintained in the management of spinal lesions.
Occasionally, en bloc resection is required for lesions in the spine.

Management
Given the potential for aggressive behavior and bone destruction, osteoblastoma must
be managed surgically. The procedure of choice depends on the location and
aggressiveness of the tumor. Intralesional curettage and en bloc resection are the most
commonly performed procedures (Figure 9).
Intralesional curettage is adequate in most patients with osteoblastoma. To minimize the
risk of recurrence, curettage should be extended to normal bone with the use of a high-
speed burr. Complete surgical removal is necessary to decrease the risk of recurrence,
which may be as high as 25% after intralesional curettage alone.1 Thermal (cryotherapy

or argon beam coagulation) and chemical (phenol) adjuvants may improve local control
after intralesional excision. Bone graft or cementation should be performed if indicated.2
In appropriate patients, en bloc resection is an effective approach for locally aggressive
and large tumors. Recurrent lesions after intralesional curettage should be managed via
en bloc resection. En bloc resection also is the preferred surgical approach for lesions in
expendable bones (ie, ribs, clavicle, and fibula).
Parosteal Osteoma
Overview
A rare, self-limiting deposition of reactive bone on the surface of the bone
Epidemiology
Demographics
Adults, most commonly in their thirties or forties.
Females are more commonly affected than males.

Epidemiology
An osteoma is a benign, bone-forming tumor that arises from membranous bones.1 It
exhibits a mature bony structure with a well-demarcated smooth border. Osteomas are
classified as ivory (compact) or spongy (trabecular) based on their dominant
radiographic features. They typically are observed in patients in their fifties. Multiple
studies have demonstrated that females are more commonly affected than males, with a
female-male ratio of 3:1.1
Etiology
Genetics/etiology

No known cause, but a history of trauma often is reported.
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History
Clinical presentation
Long history of gradual swelling or dull pain
Occasionally, incidental radiographic findings are present.
Classically, osteomas are found in the craniofacial bones. Rarely, they present in other parts
of the skeleton, including the long bones (tibia, femur), pelvis, and vertebrae.
Multiple osteomas are associated with Gardner syndrome (autosomal dominant), which also
includes colonic polyps, fibromatosis, cutaneous lesions, and subcutaneous lesions.

Patient History
The skull is commonly involved, and the osteoma presents as a slow-growing, bony
prominence. Osteomas also can form inside a sinus cavity. This may result in headaches,
recurrent sinusitis, and visual changes. Orbital involvement also may be observed in

reported in soft tissue, including the hand.
